Four AB

GeometryCirclesArea
What it shows: A circle sits around a dot in the corner where the two lines cross, and those lines cut it into four pieces.
How to play: Drag the yellow dot to move the circle, slide the bar to change its size, and tick the box to see two extra lines.
Look for the math

The two axes cut the circle into four pieces. Add the pieces in quadrants 1 and 3, subtract those in 2 and 4, and the answer turns out not to depend on the size of the circle — as long as the circle is big enough.

The four pieces

Let the centre be P = (a, b) with a > 0 and b > 0, and let the radius be r. The area of the circle in each of the four quadrants is S1, S2, S3, S4. The problem asks for

S1 − S2 + S3 − S4 = 4ab   when   r > √(a² + b²).

That square-root condition says the circle swallows a whole rectangle with corners (0,0) and (2a,2b); its farthest corners are each √(a²+b²) from P.

Why the pieces cancel

Draw the two extra lines x = 2a and y = 2b (the tick box in the picture). Together with the axes they split the disk into a central rectangle 2a × 2b and eight curved bits. The disk is symmetric about its centre P = (a,b), so reflection in x = a or y = b pairs every curved bit with an equal one in a quadrant of the opposite sign. By symmetry all those pairs cancel in the alternating sum. Only the middle rectangle is left, with area 2a × 2b = 4ab.

The logic test checked this at every small whole-number pair (a,b) and thousands of radii: equality holds exactly when r ≥ √(a²+b²). Slide the radius below that mark and the displayed sum falls short of 4ab, as it should.

The same answer in one integral

The alternating sum is the integral of sign(x)sign(y) over the disk. Slice the disk into horizontal chords of half-height √(r² − v²). Each chord contributes 2 min(a, √(r² − v²)) sign(v + b), so

S1 − S2 + S3 − S4 = 4 ∫0b min(a, √(r² − t²)) dt.

The integrand switches from a to the circle's half-height at t = √(r² − a²). If the radius is large enough, that switch happens past t = b, so the integrand is simply a all the way and the integral is 4ab. This is the same cancellation in algebraic clothes.

About the original applet

The cut-the-knot page still embeds the Java applet. Its canvas put P at (w/6, h/8) from the origin and chose an initial radius √(a²+b²) + floor(min(a,b)/10); its scroll bar ran from 0 to 100 in practice (declared maximum 105 with extent 5) and set the radius to 2 × step × value/100. Here that scroll bar is a percent slider, the starting values are the same, and P is kept in the first quadrant as the puzzle asks. The applet's internal "about" text was a leftover naming a different proof (Pythagorean Theorem, Proof #36) and changes nothing, so it is not reproduced. The live HTML states the radius condition with a square root; a plain-text copy of the page can drop the radical, so the logic test uses the square-root version.

Tick Show extra, then slide the radius down until the sum stops matching 4ab. Push it back up past √(a²+b²) and watch the answer snap to 4ab again.
